$comment: G9. The aggregate Scorecard score is a risk-weighted average that EXCLUDES checks returning '?', so it can fall for doing things right. This file is what is actually gated: a per-check minimum for the checks that reflect real risk in a knowledge repository. gate-scorecard-threshold.sh also verifies that the two tables under '## G9 — Repository quality metric' in docs/gate-requirements.md still say exactly what this file says, check for check and number for number, so the rule and its documentation cannot drift apart.

checks.why: A single pull_request_target with an untrusted checkout is the exact CSA-documented chain.
An over-permissioned GITHUB_TOKEN is what turns an injection into a compromise.
Tags are mutable and have been repointed at malicious commits in the wild.
A knowledge repository has no reason to contain binaries.
A security tool without a disclosure policy is a contradiction.

not_gated_here.why: Scorecard reads the protection block through an API call that needs administration scope. The workflow token does not have it and will not be given it: that means a personal access token stored as a secret in a public security repository, which .github/workflows/protection-drift.yml already reasoned about and refused as a larger surface than the problem it solves. So from CI this check returns -1 on every run, and -1 is COULD NOT MEASURE, which is how G9 came to exit 2 on every push since it started gating. Measured once with a maintainer token it is 3, not the 8 that was declared - so the threshold was never reachable either, and resolving the -1 would only have turned a permanent 2 into a permanent 1. The property the threshold was written for - nobody pushes directly to main - is enforced and is checked; it is checked by the scripts below rather than by this number.
not_gated_here.published_as: Its live score is printed by this gate on every run, so a fall is visible even though it does not block.

aggregate.$comment: The aggregate is recorded, not gated on its level - only on its movement. The baseline lives in a file a human edits: a workflow that could rewrite its own baseline could ratchet itself down one run at a time.
